\chapter{Venir --- Coming}
\label{ch:spanish-venir}
\hlchaptermodality{73}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that I come, and hear the stem break in the other two forms.}

vengo, then vienes and viene with the ie break.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[venir]{venir — coming with three singular forms}

\label{lesson:ES-C13-venir}



\begin{quote}
You can say \textbf{salgo de Madrid}, and you already know \textbf{tengo, tienes, tiene}. Now learn \textbf{venir}, “to come,” inside exactly the same three singular persons.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
The \textbf{g} in \textbf{vengo} is hard. In \textbf{vienes} and \textbf{viene}, let \textbf{ie} move as one smooth vowel sequence.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{venir} descends from Latin \textbf{venīre}, “to come.” English \textbf{convene} means “come together”; an \textbf{event} is something that “comes out”; and \textbf{adventure} passed through the idea of what may “come to” a person. The recurring \textbf{ven-} or \textbf{vent-} shape marks this old coming family.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one known comparison, still singular}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{present of \textbf{venir}} & \textbf{known \textbf{tener} comparison} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{vengo} & \textbf{tengo} \\
tú & \textbf{vienes} & \textbf{tienes} \\
él / ella / usted & \textbf{viene} & \textbf{tiene} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say \textbf{vengo · vienes · viene}. The learned singular forms line up closely with \textbf{tengo · tienes · tiene}: the \textbf{yo} form ends in \textbf{-go}, while the other two show \textbf{ie}. This comparison describes two complete learned sets; it does not introduce a plural “boot” table or license guesses about other verbs.

Now contrast leaving and coming with known \textbf{de} and Madrid:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Salgo de Madrid.} — “I leave Madrid.”
  \item \textbf{Vengo de Madrid.} — “I come from Madrid.”
  \item \textbf{Vienes de Madrid.} — “You come from Madrid.”
\end{itemize}

Plural persons and free-standing arrival vocabulary wait for later lessons.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “venir — vengo, vienes, viene”
  \item “Vengo de Madrid.”
  \item “vengo / tengo — vienes / tienes”
\end{itemize}
